precautions.title: 🧲 Core Overheating & Thermal Dissipation
precautions.description: Continuous cyclic magnetization causes high hysteresis/eddy-current losses. Do not operate at peak excitation currents for longer than 3 consecutive minutes.

theory.title: 📖 Theory — Magnetic Hysteresis & Core Loss
theory.objective: To investigate the non-linear relationship between magnetic field strength (H) and flux density (B), record the closed B–H loop, and evaluate energy loss per magnetization cycle.
points: Ferromagnetic materials consist of microscopic magnetic domains. In an unmagnetized state, domain orientations are randomly distributed with zero net external magnetization.
Applying an external magnetic field H aligns these domains in the direction of the field, causing flux density B to increase non-linearly up to saturation.
When the external field is reversed, domain rotation is resisted by microscopic lattice friction and pinning sites; magnetization lags behind the field, giving rise to 'hysteresis'.
The area enclosed by the closed B–H trajectory represents electrical energy permanently converted into thermal energy per unit volume during each AC cycle.

formulaDetails.name: Applied Magnetizing Field Strength (Ampere's Law)

variables.name: Magnetic Field Strength
variables.desc: Magnetomotive force applied per unit magnetic path length

variables.name: Number of Coil Turns
variables.desc: Number of wire loops wound onto the magnetic core

variables.name: Excitation Current
variables.desc: Instantaneous AC current passing through the excitation winding

variables.name: Mean Magnetic Path Length
variables.desc: Average circumferential path length of magnetic flux through the core

formulaDetails.description: Describes the primary magnetomotive force driving magnetic flux through the core material. Increasing winding turns or current proportionately intensifies the magnetizing field.
formulaDetails.physicalSignificance: Controlled directly via the laboratory AC excitation voltage and coil configuration.

formulaDetails.name: Magnetic Flux Density (Constitutive Relation)
formulaDetails.formula: B = μ · H = μ₀ · μ_r · H = μ₀ · (H + M)

variables.name: Magnetic Flux Density
variables.desc: Density of magnetic lines of force per unit cross-sectional area

variables.name: Permeability of Free Space
variables.desc: Fundamental physical magnetic constant of vacuum

variables.name: Relative Permeability
variables.desc: Amplification factor of the ferromagnetic material compared to air

variables.name: Magnetization Vector
variables.desc: Net magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of the specimen

formulaDetails.description: Measures the resulting magnetic induction inside the core. In ferromagnetic materials, μ_r is not constant but varies dynamically along the non-linear S-shaped hysteresis curve.
formulaDetails.physicalSignificance: Soft materials (like silicon steel) exhibit steep initial slopes (high permeability), while hard magnets maintain high remanence even when H returns to zero.

formulaDetails.name: Hysteresis Energy Loss per Unit Volume
formulaDetails.formula: w_h = ∮ B · dH = Area of B–H Hysteresis Loop

variables.name: Energy Loss Density per Cycle
variables.desc: Mechanical/magnetic energy dissipated as heat in one AC cycle

variables.name: Closed Contour Integral
variables.desc: Area enclosed within the complete B–H curve

formulaDetails.description: Each AC cycle drives magnetic domains back and forth against internal pinning barriers, irreversibly converting electrical power into heat within the specimen core.
formulaDetails.physicalSignificance: Transformer cores use narrow sigmoid silicon steel to minimize loop area, whereas permanent magnets require large rhombic loop areas for high coercivity.

formulaDetails.name: Total Hysteresis Power Loss (Steinmetz Equation)

variables.name: Total Power Dissipation
variables.desc: Total rate of heat generation across entire core

variables.name: Excitation Frequency
variables.desc: Frequency of alternating magnetic field cycles

variables.name: Peak Flux Density
variables.desc: Maximum amplitude of magnetic flux density during the cycle

variables.name: Core Volume
variables.desc: Physical volume of the ferromagnetic material

formulaDetails.description: Calculates the total continuous thermal wattage generated. Power loss scales directly with AC operating frequency and strongly with peak induction B_max.
formulaDetails.physicalSignificance: Directly explains why high-frequency magnetic devices require specialized low-loss core materials to prevent thermal runaway.

workedExample.title: Standard Transformer Core Worked Example
workedExample.given: AC Voltage = 12.0 V, Turns N = 250, Frequency f = 50 Hz, Core Area = 4.0 cm², Path l_m = 0.25 m
steps: 1. Core Area: A = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²; Core Volume V_core = A × l_m = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³
2. Excitation Current: I_max ≈ 0.12 A  ==>  H_max = (250 × 0.12) / 0.25 = 120.0 A/m
4. Measured Sigmoid Loop Area: w_h ≈ 45.0 J/m³ per cycle
5. Total Power Loss: P_h = 45.0 J/m³ × 50 Hz × 0.0001 m³ = 0.225 W = 225 mW
workedExample.conclusion: A silicon steel transformer core dissipates 225 mW of continuous thermal power under these conditions, operating within safe temperature tolerances.
